To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) past-tense generation in English involves a regularity effect when the task is to generate the past from the verb stem; (2) this regularity effect is not reliable when the task is past generation from action picture; and (3) a single-mechansim model of inflectional processing can account for the task-dependent pattern of results.
the regularity effect is task-dependent, and the magnitude of the effect varies as a function of task and item frequency.

(a) when participants are asked to produce the past tense from the stem of the verb, they show a reliable regularity effect, but (b) when participants are given a picture and asked to produce the appropriate verb form, the regularity effect is not reliable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the mental processes that underpin the generation of inflectional forms.
the relationship between the form and meaning of verbs and the processing consequences of this relationship.
how the processing of irregular and regular verbs is affected by the nature of the task and how these findings can be accommodated in computational models of inflection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are two mechanisms for verb inflection: the first mechanism is the rule-governed regular process; the second mechanism is the irregular process.
the results from this study are consistent with a single-mechanic model of inflection.

dual- and single-mechanisms models of inflectional processing are equally able to account for the behavioural data, but the models differ with respect to their predictions for the magnitude of the effect in the meaning generation task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the task used to investigate the regularity effect is crucial for the results obtained.
the past-tense generation task from meaning does not support dual-mechanism models.
the past tense of English verbs can be generated from either form or meaning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single-mechanical model can account for the behavioural data, and that this model provides a better account of the task-dependent effects observed than dual-mechanism models.
the task used in studies of inflectional processing has important implications for the conclusions that can be drawn about how inflectional morphology is represented in the mental lexicon.
the task used to elicit inflectional behaviour can have a profound impact on the pattern of results, and thus on the theoretical interpretation of the data.
